props.title: Drive

sections.content: Let's not confuse Mark Dacascos' Drive (1997) with Nicolas Winding Refn's 2011 Ryan Gosling vehicle. This late-90s martial arts gem combines Hong Kong-style action with American B-movie charm. Director Steve Wang, who cut his teeth on practical effects for films like Predator (1987), brings his creature-feature expertise to create stunning practical fight sequences. The film follows Toby Wong (Dacascos), a martial artist with a bio-engine implant that enhances his fighting abilities, as he tries to escape agents who want to reclaim the technology.

sections.content: Drive emerged during a fascinating transition period in American martial arts cinema. The mid-90s saw Hong Kong influences seeping into Hollywood, years before The Matrix (1999) would revolutionize action choreography. Wang's direction shows clear inspiration from Hong Kong directors like Tsui Hark and John Woo, particularly in the use of wire-enhanced kicks and stylized gunplay. The film's practical effects and stunt work stand in stark contrast to today's CGI-heavy action sequences.

What sets Drive apart is its playful tone and buddy comedy elements. While contemporary martial arts films like Mortal Kombat (1995) and Double Dragon (1994) leaned into grim self-seriousness, Drive embraces its B-movie roots. The chemistry between Dacascos and co-star Kadeem Hardison creates a dynamic reminiscent of Big Trouble in Little China (1986), where humor and action complement rather than undercut each other. sections.content: Dacascos brings a unique physical presence to Drive that deserves special attention. His background in multiple martial arts styles - including capoeira and kung fu - allows for varied fight choreography that stands out from the kickboxing-heavy American martial arts films of the era like Kickboxer (1989) or American Ninja (1985). His performance influenced later martial arts stars and can be seen as a precursor to the more acrobatic style that would become prominent in the 2000s.
